clue.text: Accessories that secure rider's bags?

parts.note: surface reading: the panniers or saddlebags a cyclist carries; setter's reading: bags is slang for trousers, and these fasteners hold a cyclist's trouser legs clear of the chain

explanation.walkthrough: Bags is British slang for trousers, so the accessories keep a cyclist's trouser hems tight at the ankle.
explanation.definitionFit: These metal or elastic bands clamp a cyclist's trouser legs so the cloth does not catch in the chain.

clue.text: Bovine expert by a sawn-off log

indicators.note: something sawn off has had its end cut away, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast with expert knowledge
taken as written
taken as written before the cut

explanation.surface: A cattle specialist stands beside a stubby log.
explanation.walkthrough: BUFF + A + LO(g), the log losing its end.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffalo is a large wild ox, a member of the cattle family, so it is a bovine animal.

clue.text: Six-footer slips in this sport

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a chirping insect, which has six legs
second meaning: the bat-and-ball game whose slips are close catching positions beside the wicketkeeper

explanation.walkthrough: Six-footer suggests a tall person, but it means a creature with six feet. In the game, slips are fielders standing near the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a leaping insect, which like every insect has six legs, and the English bat-and-ball game with fielding slips.

clue.text: Gloomy, say "hip hip hooray!" only twice?

parts.note: each hip hip hooray is one cheer, the call usually given three times
giving the call twice instead of the customary three times means one fewer

explanation.surface: A half-hearted crowd manages only two rounds of applause, a glum occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: Three cheers is the custom, so stopping at two is one CHEER LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerless describes something dreary and joyless, a close synonym of gloomy.

clue.text: Gems that page has dropped off for nobles

indicators.note: something that has dropped off is no longer there, so that letter is removed

parts.note: pearls are precious gems
P is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A necklace has lost its jewels, apparently traded for titles.
explanation.walkthrough: PEARLS without its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Earls are titled members of the British peerage, so they are aristocrats ranking among the nobility.

clue.text: Handsome politician?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: generous, as in a handsome sum
second meaning: a member of a party of that name

explanation.walkthrough: Handsome looks like good-looking, but here it means generous, as a handsome tip is a big one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means lavish or generous in amount, and as a noun it names a member of the Liberal party.

clue.text: Leading cleric and soldier (Mike, not Victor)

indicators.note: 'Mike, not Victor' says the letter for Mike goes where the letter for Victor stood in the soldier word

parts.note: a private is the lowest rank of soldier
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A senior churchman and a serviceman stand together, with a note about two people called Mike and Victor.
explanation.walkthrough: Take PRIVATE, a soldier, and swap its V (Victor) for M (Mike), as 'not' directs.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate is an archbishop or the chief bishop of a province, the highest-ranking churchman there.

clue.text: I elect a criminal to break into high street shop for neckwear

indicators.note: the shuffled letters break into the shop, so they are placed inside its name

parts.note: Boots is a chain of chemist's shops found on most British high streets

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are crooked, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone voted in turns crook and breaks into a shop to steal some neckwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a burglary, but 'break into' only means placing the shuffled letters inside the shop's name; Boots is a British chain of chemist's shops on almost every high street.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootlace ties are thin cord neckties worn with a slide clasp, a type of neckwear.

clue.text: Echo accompanying Rotten and Vicious? Stop playing because of it

parts.note: food that has gone rotten is off
Sid Vicious was the bass player of the Sex Pistols alongside Johnny Rotten
Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A tribute to the Sex Pistols, Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious, then a call to stop the music.
explanation.walkthrough: Echo accompanies the other two by coming after them. Rotten and Vicious point to the punk band, but only Vicious is used for a name.
explanation.definitionFit: In football and rugby the referee halts the game when a player is caught in an illegal forward position, the offence named by the answer.

clue.text: Surrounded by religious leaders at first, talks and talks

indicators.note: being surrounded means having others all around you, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: rabbis are Jewish religious leaders

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter only of the word that follows

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A meeting of clergy where somebody talks on and on, hemmed in by them.
explanation.walkthrough: T sits inside RABBIS. To rabbit, or rabbit on, is British slang for talking at length.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to rabbit on is to chatter endlessly, so rabbits is a verb meaning chats or prattles.

clue.text: Bloomer from fool, perhaps — Shakespeare?

parts.note: a fool is a fruit-and-cream dessert, an example of a sweet
the playwright's first name

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's fools make a blunder, a bloomer from the clown.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomer reads as a mistake, but it is something that blooms. A fool is a British pudding, and sweet is the British word for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet william is a garden plant with clustered flowers, so it is a flowering plant, something that blooms.

clue.text: Follower of song by Queen

parts.note: a track is a song on an album
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A fan of a song by the rock band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen looks like the band, but it is the royal abbreviation ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracker follows the trail or movements of something, so a tracker is a pursuer who follows.

clue.text: Which women may change after the match?

definitions.text: Which women may change after the match?

parts.note: surface reading: players changing clothes after a sports fixture; setter's reading: a match is a marriage, after which a bride traditionally takes her husband's family name

explanation.walkthrough: Match sounds sporting, but it means a wedding. Many brides adopt the husband's family name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the family name, which a bride traditionally gives up for her husband's after marrying.

clue.text: At last, Cassandra Trotter is up

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the next word only

parts.note: the final letter of the name
a trotter is a pig's foot

explanation.surface: Cassandra Trotter, Rodney's wife in the sitcom Only Fools and Horses, has finally got out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Only Fools and Horses is a classic British sitcom about the Trotter family; a trotter is also a pig's foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Afoot means happening or in progress, as does up in the sense of what's up.

clue.text: Spreadsheet program given capital

parts.note: Microsoft's spreadsheet software
lent means handed over for a while

explanation.surface: Accountants are handed a spreadsheet program along with the funding.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like money, but it is an old-fashioned British exclamation of approval.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital is dated British slang for splendid or first-rate, so it is a synonym of excellent.

clue.text: This out of order, I can't shop?

definitions.text: This out of order, I can't shop?

indicators.note: out of order means the letters are not in their proper sequence, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shopper laments that the machine is broken, so they cannot buy anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' rearranges the letters of I CANT SHOP; the whole clue also describes the result, since a broken cash machine leaves you without money to spend.
explanation.definitionFit: A cashpoint is a British term for an ATM; when it is broken you cannot withdraw money to go shopping.

clue.text: Football team regularly seeks a break

parts.note: a football side has eleven players

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A football side periodically tries for a breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack break, named for eleven o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a short pause for tea and biscuits in the late morning, so it is a break.

clue.text: Country where son is in public school, flipping marvellous!

indicators.note: one letter being in something means it sits inside it

parts.note: Eton is a famous English public school
S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: A1 means first-class, and the digit 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A parent boasts that their son is at a top school, which is wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is an old fee-paying school; Eton is the best known. Flipping looks like a mild British oath but turns A1 round.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic nation, a sovereign state in northern Europe, so it is a country.

clue.text: Serious attention given to refuge

parts.note: to give an ear is to pay attention
a nest is a safe retreat

explanation.surface: A sober note on how much care goes into providing shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest describes someone sincere and intent, so it is a synonym of serious in manner.

clue.text: Injure back before international in Florida city

indicators.note: back means going the opposite way, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: to maim is to injure badly
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A footballer hurts his back ahead of an international match in Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: Back looks like the body part, but it signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: Miami is a large city on the Atlantic coast of the US state of Florida.

clue.text: One can expect to be charged after entering arena

definitions.text: One can expect to be charged after entering arena

parts.words: expect to be charged after entering arena
parts.note: surface reading: someone who will face criminal charges or a bill; setter's reading: in the bullring the bull rushes at the man who fights it

explanation.walkthrough: Charged suggests a court or a price, but it is the bull charging.
explanation.definitionFit: A matador is the bullfighter who faces and kills the bull, which runs at him in the ring.

clue.text: Ace surreal art — save mainly as internet forum icons

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

indicators.note: a surreal picture is dreamlike and distorted, so the letters are jumbled
mainly means most of it but not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written before the cut

explanation.surface: A collector of excellent surrealist art saves pictures to use as profile images online.
explanation.walkthrough: A + an anagram of ART and SAV(e).
explanation.definitionFit: An avatar is the small picture or figure representing a user on a website or in a game.

clue.text: Temporary component of teleprinter imported

indicators.note: a component is a part of a whole, so the letters are a part of the following words

parts.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: A stopgap part has been brought in for an old telex machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim means provisional, serving for the meantime until something permanent is arranged.

clue.text: Tips from male actor knowing ER producer

indicators.note: the tips of words are their front ends, so only the leading letters are taken

parts.note: the leading letters of the three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice from a savvy actor to the makers of the hospital drama ER.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the American hospital drama series, here simply read as its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker is someone who manufactures or creates things, so a synonym of producer.

clue.text: Fat lip after tripping in front of large hazard

indicators.note: someone who trips falls about, so the letters come out in a tumbled order

parts.note: the letters rearranged
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone got a swollen lip from a fall over a big obstacle.
explanation.walkthrough: A fat lip is the natural result of tripping, which hides the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitfall is a hidden danger or trap, so a hazard in the sense of an unforeseen risk.

clue.text: Newspaper cover showing part of cruise ship

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
to deck is to cover or dress something up

explanation.surface: A tabloid's front page features a liner.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover suggests a front page, but it is the verb to deck.
explanation.definitionFit: A sun deck is the open top deck of a liner where passengers sunbathe, so it is part of the vessel.

clue.text: State I must appear before final bit from Jonathan Ross?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the final bit of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the name
Diana Ross is the American soul singer

explanation.surface: A guest is told to appear on the British chat show of Jonathan Ross.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Ross is a British TV presenter, but the clue splits him: Ross is Diana Ross. The question mark hints at Indiana Jones too.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Naval officer's team drained of energy as Starmer rambles

indicators.note: to ramble is to wander aimlessly, so the letters stray into a new order
drained of means emptied of, so the letter for energy is removed

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A naval officer's crew grows tired while Keir Starmer, the British Prime Minister, gives a long rambling speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drained of' takes E (energy) out of TEAM to leave TAM; 'rambles' rearranges TAM with AS and STARMER.
explanation.definitionFit: A master-at-arms is the senior rating in charge of discipline and policing aboard a warship.
